title: Temporal Coherence in Optics
short_intro: Temporal coherence characterizes the phase correlation of a light wave at a single point in space at two different instants of time. It is a fundamental measure of the monochromaticity and frequency stability of an optical source.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Qualitative understanding of coherence, interference conditions, distinction between temporal and spatial coherence, and path difference limits in classical interferometers like Michelson.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Rigorous mathematical formulation using mutual coherence functions, power spectral density via the Wiener-Khinchin theorem, coherence time, coherence length, and wave packet analysis.

prerequisites: Fourier transforms and frequency spectrum analysis
Wave optics and path-to-phase difference conversion

concept_notes.heading: Definition and Physical Origin
bullets: Temporal coherence measures the correlation between electric field vectors E(t) and E(t + τ) at the same spatial point.
It arises due to the finite bandwidth (Δν) or frequency spread of real optical sources.
Perfect monochromatic light possesses infinite temporal coherence, whereas actual sources emit wave trains of finite duration.

concept_notes.heading: Coherence Time and Coherence Length
bullets: Coherence time (τ<sub>c</sub>) is the maximum time interval over which a predictable phase relationship is maintained, given by τ<sub>c</sub> ≈ 1 / Δν.
Coherence length (L<sub>c</sub>) is the spatial extent of the wave train, expressed as L<sub>c</sub> = cτ<sub>c</sub> = c / Δν.
For light with a mean wavelength λ<sub>0</sub> and wavelength spread Δλ, L<sub>c</sub> ≈ λ<sub>0</sub><sup>2</sup> / Δλ.

concept_notes.heading: Degree of Temporal Coherence
bullets: Quantified by the complex degree of temporal coherence γ<sub>12</sub>(τ), defined via the normalized auto-correlation function of the electric field.

Fringe visibility V in a two-beam interferometer is directly proportional to the magnitude of the degree of temporal coherence: V = 2√(I<sub>1</sub>I<sub>2</sub>) / (I<sub>1</sub> + I<sub>2</sub>) |γ<sub>12</sub>(τ)|.
Interference fringes vanish when the optical path difference exceeds the coherence length of the source.

concept_notes.heading: Relation with Frequency Spectrum (Wiener-Khinchin Theorem)
bullets: The temporal coherence function and the power spectral density of a light source form a Fourier transform pair.
A broader spectral width (Δν) results in a narrower coherence function and shorter coherence length.
Laser sources have extremely narrow linewidths, yielding coherence lengths of meters to kilometers.

derivations.title: Derivation of Coherence Length from Wavelength Spread
derivations.conditions: Quasi-monochromatic source with mean wavelength λ<sub>0</sub> and spectral width Δλ
steps: Express frequency ν in terms of wavelength: ν = c / λ.
Differentiate to find the frequency spread corresponding to wavelength spread: dν = (c / λ<sup>2</sup>) dλ, hence Δν = (c / λ<sub>0</sub><sup>2</sup>) Δλ.
Use the definition of coherence time τ<sub>c</sub> = 1 / Δν to substitute Δν.
Multiply coherence time by the speed of light c to obtain coherence length L<sub>c</sub> = c τ<sub>c</sub>.

derivations.title: Relation between Fringe Visibility and Path Difference
derivations.conditions: Two-beam interference with unequal path lengths producing an optical path difference (OPD) Δx
steps: Define the time delay corresponding to the OPD as τ = Δx / c.
Express the intensity in the interference pattern as I(τ) = I<sub>0</sub> [1 + |γ(τ)| cos(k c τ)], where γ(τ) is the degree of temporal coherence.
Identify maximum and minimum intensities: I<sub>max</sub> = I<sub>0</sub> (1 + |γ(τ)|) and I<sub>min</sub> = I<sub>0</sub> (1 - |γ(τ)|).

graphs_and_experiments.title: Michelson Interferometer fringe visibility vs Path Difference
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A damped cosine oscillation curve where fringe visibility V decreases monotonically from 1 to 0 as path difference Δx increases.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Demonstrates that interference fringes wash out when the path difference exceeds the coherence length of the source.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Tested conceptually to determine coherence length of sodium lamps or lasers.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Power Spectral Density and Coherence Function
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A Gaussian or Lorentzian spectral profile Δν matched against the corresponding Fourier-transformed temporal envelope τ<sub>c</sub>.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Shows inverse relationship between spectral width in frequency domain and temporal extent in time domain.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Used in PGT numericals relating linewidth to coherence time.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Wave Packet Train representation
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Series of finite sinusoidal wave packets of length L<sub>c</sub> separated by random phase jumps.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Illustrates that thermal sources emit independent wave bursts with random initial phases.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Helps clarify why incoherent sources cannot produce stable interference over long path differences.

solved_numericals.question: Calculate the coherence length of a sodium light source emitting at mean wavelength 589 nm with a spectral wavelength spread of 0.6 nm.
solution_steps: Identify given values: λ<sub>0</sub> = 589 nm = 589 \times 10<sup>-9</sup> m, Δλ = 0.6 nm = 0.6 \times 10<sup>-9</sup> m.
Apply the formula for coherence length: L<sub>c</sub> = λ<sub>0</sub><sup>2</sup> / Δλ.

solved_numericals.question: A laser source has a frequency bandwidth of 2 MHz. Find its coherence time and coherence length.
solution_steps: Identify given frequency bandwidth: Δν = 2 MHz = 2 \times 10<sup>6</sup> Hz.
Calculate coherence length using L<sub>c</sub> = c τ<sub>c</sub> taking c = 3 \times 10<sup>8</sup> m/s.
solved_numericals.answer: Coherence time = 5 \times 10^-7 s, Coherence length = 150 m

solved_numericals.question: In a Michelson interferometer experiment using a spectral line, fringes disappear when the movable mirror is translated by 0.15 mm. Estimate the spectral width (Δλ) of the source if its mean wavelength is 600 nm.
solution_steps: Note that fringe disappearance occurs when path difference Δx = 2 × (mirror translation d) = 2 \times 0.15 mm = 0.30 mm = 3 \times 10<sup>-4</sup> m.
Equate coherence length L<sub>c</sub> to path difference: L<sub>c</sub> = Δx = 3 \times 10<sup>-4</sup> m.
Use formula L<sub>c</sub> = λ<sub>0</sub><sup>2</sup> / Δλ to solve for Δλ.

assumptions_and_limitations: Assumes quasi-monochromatic light where spectral width is much smaller than mean frequency (Δν \ll \nu<sub>0</sub>).
Coherence length formulas represent order-of-magnitude estimates based on Fourier transform limits rather than exact lineshape profiles unless specified as Gaussian or Lorentzian.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Temporal coherence depends on the physical size and spatial separation of the light source pinholes.
common_misconceptions.correct: Temporal coherence depends strictly on the frequency spectrum (monochromaticity) of the source, whereas spatial coherence depends on source size.
common_misconceptions.why: Spatial and temporal coherence are orthogonal properties; temporal relates to time delays at a single point, spatial relates to phase correlations at different points.

common_misconceptions.wrong: A thermal source like an incandescent bulb has a long coherence length because it appears bright.
common_misconceptions.correct: Thermal sources have broad emission bandwidths, resulting in very short coherence lengths (typically micrometers).
common_misconceptions.why: Brightness is related to intensity, not frequency purity or coherence.

quick_revision: Temporal coherence is the correlation of a wave with its time-delayed self (τ = Δx / c).
Coherence time τ<sub>c</sub> = 1 / Δν and coherence length L<sub>c</sub> = λ<sub>0</sub><sup>2</sup> / Δλ.
Fringe visibility vanishes when optical path difference exceeds coherence length.
